summary.text: A colloid is a mixture in which microscopically dispersed insoluble particles of one substance are suspended throughout another substance.
It has a dispersed phase, the suspended particles, and a continuous phase, the medium they are suspended in.
Unlike a solution, where solute and solvent make up one phase, a colloid has multiple phases and bigger particles than single molecules or ions.

items.prompt: In salt water, ions are surrounded by water molecules. How does milk differ?

options.label: Its particles are globules of fat, bigger than single molecules
Its fat is dissolved into individual molecules
Its particles are ions, like the salt's
It has only a single phase, like salt water

items.explain: In a colloid such as milk the particles are globules of fat rather than individual molecules, and colloidal particles are bigger than a solution's molecules or ions.

items.prompt: Tiny particles denser than the liquid around them sink over time. If they were less dense, what would happen?

options.label: They would stay spread out evenly forever
They would dissolve into single molecules
They would float to the top
They would sink more slowly but still reach the bottom

items.explain: Particles denser than the medium sediment, while less dense ones cream, floating to the top.

items.prompt: Of two cloudy mixtures, the one with bigger particles settles out faster. Why?

options.label: Bigger particles carry a stronger electric charge
Bigger particles have less Brownian motion to counteract settling
Bigger particles dissolve into the liquid
Bigger particles are always denser

items.explain: Larger particles have a greater tendency to sediment because they have smaller Brownian motion to counteract the movement.

items.prompt: Why can some colloids look translucent?

options.label: Their particles soak up the light entirely
Their dissolved ions glow in the dark
They contain no particles, only ions
Their particles scatter light, the Tyndall effect

items.explain: Some colloids are translucent because of the Tyndall effect, the scattering of light by particles in the colloid.

items.prompt: Particles in a mixture are about 5 μm across. Can it be a colloidal suspension?

options.label: Probably not, since particles larger than 1 μm tend to sediment
Yes, since any size of suspended particle counts
Yes, since bigger particles stay suspended best
No, since colloids must be fully dissolved

items.explain: There is an upper limit on colloidal particle diameter, because particles larger than 1 μm tend to sediment.

items.prompt: A cook stirs corn starch, a hydrocolloid, into a liquid. What can hydrocolloids do to water?

options.label: Lower its viscosity so it runs freely
Turn it into a gas
Raise its viscosity or make it gel
Pull the water out of it

items.explain: Hydrocolloids are dispersible in water and change its rheology by raising the viscosity and/or inducing gelation; corn starch is one.

paragraphs.heading: What a colloid is
paragraphs.text: A colloid is a mixture in which tiny insoluble particles of one substance are spread out and held suspended through another. It has two parts: the dispersed phase, which is the suspended particles, and the continuous phase, which is the medium holding them. Some definitions require that medium to be a liquid, while others also count aerosols and gels.

paragraphs.heading: A matter of size
paragraphs.text: Calling something colloidal means its particles measure, in at least one direction, roughly between 1 nanometre and 1 micrometre. Not all three dimensions need to fall in that range, and the limits are not rigid. There is still an upper bound, since particles larger than 1 μm tend to sink, and the mixture would then stop counting as a colloidal suspension. Everett, who wrote the IUPAC definition, stressed that colloids are often better understood through examples than through strict definitions.

paragraphs.heading: Colloid versus solution
paragraphs.text: In a solution, solute and solvent make up only one phase, and the solute is individual molecules or ions. A colloid has a dispersed and a continuous phase, and its particles are bigger. When salt dissolves in water, its Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions end up surrounded by water molecules. In milk, by contrast, the particles are globules of fat rather than single fat molecules. Because it has more than one phase, a colloid behaves very differently from a fully mixed solution.

paragraphs.heading: Light and gravity
paragraphs.text: Some colloids are translucent because their particles scatter light, which is called the Tyndall effect, while others are opaque or slightly coloured. Gravity pulls on colloidal particles as well. If the particles are denser than the medium they sediment, falling to the bottom, and if they are less dense they cream, floating to the top. Larger particles sediment more readily, since they have less Brownian motion to work against the fall.

paragraphs.heading: Forces between particles
paragraphs.text: Several forces act between colloidal particles. Hard particles can never overlap, which keeps them apart. They often carry electric charge, so they attract or repel each other. Van der Waals forces arise when shifting electron density gives a particle a temporary dipole that induces dipoles in nearby particles, which then attract; this pull is short-range and always present unless the two phases have matched refractive indexes. Polymers coating a particle's surface can add a repulsive steric force.

paragraphs.heading: Useful hydrocolloids
paragraphs.text: Hydrocolloids are chemicals, mostly polysaccharides and proteins, that disperse colloidally in water. They make water thicker or turn it into a gel. That makes them useful across foods, medicines, personal-care products and industry. Corn starch and casein are hydrocolloids that are also foods. Some can be dried after dissolving to form breath-strip films, artificial sausage casings and wound-dressing fibres.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: Colloids are studied in interface and colloid science. The field began in 1845 with Francesco Selmi, who called these mixtures pseudosolutions. Michael Faraday and Thomas Graham later widened it, and the word colloid itself dates from 1861.
